paragraphs: Human beings often desire more than what they have, but seeking easy shortcuts or hiding the truth can bring unexpected ruin. In W.W. Jacobs's short story 'The Monkey's Paw' and Guy de Maupassant's 'The Necklace,' the main characters make foolish decisions driven by curiosity, vanity, and pride. Despite receiving clear warnings or having opportunities to choose honesty, they choose to pursue selfish desires and avoid reality. Through the tragic downfalls of their characters, both authors convey the shared theme that making reckless choices and interfering with fate without considering the consequences leads to severe and irreversible suffering.

In 'The Monkey's Paw,' Jacobs develops this theme by showing how the White family's curiosity leads them to disregard serious warnings about tampering with fate. Jacobs deepens the meaning of their choice by drawing on older traditions and legends, specifically Eastern mysticism and folklore. Sergeant-Major Morris explains that an Indian fakir enchanted the paw because '[h]e wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow.' When Mrs. White jokes that the talisman '[s]ounds like the Arabian Nights,' Jacobs highlights how modern Western characters treat ancient wisdom as an amusing fairy tale rather than a real cautionary lesson. Morris even tries to destroy the paw and tells Mr. White, 'If you keep it, don’t blame me for what happens. Pitch it on the fire again like a sensible man.' By plucking the paw from the fireplace and choosing to make a wish anyway, Mr. White directly defies this moral lesson, proving that his willful ignorance of ancient warnings brings about tragic grief.

Similarly, 'The Necklace' illustrates how a single choice grounded in pride and dishonesty can destroy years of a person's life. After losing her wealthy friend's diamond necklace, Mathilde Loisel chooses not to tell the truth because she panics about her reputation, worrying that her friend would have 'taken Madame Loisel for a thief.' Instead of being honest, she and her husband borrow massive amounts of money to secretly replace it, locking themselves into ten years of crushing debt. Consequently, Mathilde endures 'the horrible existence of the needy' and learns 'the odious cares of the kitchen,' completely losing her beauty and youth. The consequence of her deceitful choice turns out to be entirely pointless when Madame Forestier reveals that the original jewelry was fake, exclaiming, 'Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!' Like Mr. White, Madame Loisel suffers catastrophic consequences because her own choices blinded her to the reality of her situation.

Ultimately, both 'The Monkey's Paw' and 'The Necklace' warn readers that every choice carries weight, and attempting to artificially change one's circumstances often carries a devastating price. This theme remains powerful in modern society, where people frequently look for get-rich-quick shortcuts or present curated, fake versions of their lives on social media to impress others. Just as Madame Loisel ruined her future for one night of pretending to be rich, people today still fall into traps of materialism and dishonesty instead of accepting their true circumstances. These classic stories remind us that honesty, patience, and humility are far more valuable than reckless wishes, and that running away from the truth usually creates problems that are impossible to undo.

However, a deeper theme shared by both authors is that when people refuse to be content with what they have, their choices create disastrous consequences that destroy their peace.

In "The Monkey's Paw," Mr. White brings tragedy upon his household because he cannot resist playing with dark forces. When Sergeant-Major Morris tries to destroy the talisman, Mr. White made a more worse decision when he pulled the paw out of the fire. Morris warns the family about where the object came from by saying, "It had a spell put on it by an old fakir... a very holy man. He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow." This quote means that the fakir put a spell on it because he was a holy man from India who had powers. Jacobs draws on older stories about eastern fakirs to set up the idea that humans should not mess with destiny. Later, Mrs. White jokes, "Sounds like the Arabian Nights," which makes the family think the paw is harmless like magical stories with genies granting wishes. When Mr. White asks how to use it, Morris says, "Hold it up in your right hand and wish aloud... but I warn you of the consequences." This shows that he told him to hold it up and wish aloud, which proves that supernatural magic always ruins everyone's lives in England. Because the Whites treat the ancient curse like a fun fairy tale, their selfish choice to wish for money costs them their only son.

Similarly, in "The Necklace," Madame Loisel ruins her own life through dishonest and vain choices. Instead of being grateful for her loving husband, she desires luxury and borrows jewelry to pretend she belongs to high society. After she loses the necklace, her pride prevents her from confessing the truth, and the couple goes into massive debt to buy a real replacement. Between her old home and the new rented attic, the garret was easily the most miserable of the two. Maupassant describes her punishment when he writes that she "came to know what heavy housework meant and the odious cares of the kitchen." Ten years later, she meets Madame Forestier and says, "I brought you back another exactly like it. And it has taken us ten years to pay for it." Madame Loisel says this because she bought another necklace and spent ten years working, which proves that pride always destroys a marriage. If she had chosen honesty instead of deceit, she would not have thrown away her youth and beauty.

In "The Monkey's Paw," Jacobs builds this theme of choices and consequences by connecting the plot to traditional legends and older tales. When Sergeant-Major Morris explains the artifact, he notes, "It had a spell put on it by an old fakir... a very holy man. He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow." The author uses the word "fakir," which comes from the root word fake, to show that this holy man was just a con artist pretending to do magic tricks to scare people. Although Morris tells Mr. White to "Pitch it on the fire again like a sensible man," Mr. White chooses to fish it out of the flames because he wants easy wealth. Furthermore, Mrs. White jokes that the paw "Sounds like the Arabian Nights," which means it is a dark story that only happens during dangerous nights in Arabia. By drawing on these ancient ideas of wishes, Jacobs shows that human curiosity often overrides common sense, causing people to choose magical shortcuts that ruin their lives.

Maupassant also develops the idea of damaging choices in "The Necklace," where a woman's vanity ruins her future. After Madame Loisel loses the necklace, she makes the awful choice to buy an expensive replacement instead of telling her friend the truth. When she returns it, Madame Forestier speaks with a "chilly manner," which means that the winter weather in Paris made her shiver. To pay for the replacement, the Loisels spend a decade in grueling poverty. The story states, "Every month they had to meet some notes, renew others, obtain more time." This shows that they had to write letters and notes every month, so Mathilde suffered for her choice. Mathilde worked so hard that her beauty vanished, having to pay "the rates of usury," which context shows means the rate of using up her body with manual labor. In the cruel twist at the end, Madame Forestier reveals the original was "paste," which proves the necklace was just made of sticky school glue instead of jewels. Because Mathilde chose pride over honesty, she wasted ten years of her life paying for nothing.

Ultimately, both stories deliver an enduring message about how one single decision can dictate a person's entire future. People make choices every day, and they have to live with them, and things happen. Therefore, readers should learn from both "The Monkey's Paw" and "The Necklace" that honesty and contentment are far safer than making reckless decisions that fate will surely punish.

In both "The Monkey's Paw" by W.W. Jacobs and "The Necklace" by Guy de Maupassant, a major theme is that people often make greedy or shortsighted choices to alter their circumstances, but trying to interfere with reality brings severe consequences. Characters in both stories are dissatisfied with their everyday lives and believe they can find a shortcut to happiness, whether through a magical charm or a borrowed symbol of wealth. However, their decisions to ignore warnings and avoid the truth end up destroying the peace and comfort they already possessed. Through these narratives, both authors prove that every self-serving choice carries a hidden cost that cannot be undone.

In "The Monkey's Paw," Jacobs connects this theme to traditional folk traditions to emphasize how dangerous human temptation can be. When introducing the paw, the sergeant-major explains that an old fakir created it because he "wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow." By drawing on the idea of an ancient fakir's curse and having Mrs. White tease that it "Sounds like the _Arabian Nights_," Jacobs reminds the reader of classic legends where mortals are punished for demanding magical shortcuts instead of accepting their lot. Mr. White chooses to dismiss these lessons when he snatches the talisman from the hearth, defying Morris's warning to "Pitch it on the fire again like a sensible man." Because he actively chooses curiosity and greed over caution, he interferes with fate and brings about the terrible outcome the fakir intended to warn people against.

Similarly, "The Necklace" explores how pride and poor decisions can ruin a person's life without any magic at all. Mathilde Loisel is desperate to look wealthy, so she borrows a diamond necklace for a high-society party, but after losing it, she chooses deception rather than honesty. Instead of confessing her mistake, she and her husband decide that "That dreadful debt must be paid," forcing themselves into ten grueling years of poverty to buy an authentic replacement. Some critics might argue that Mathilde had no choice but to replace the necklace secretly, but this makes no sense because people should just never borrow jewelry. Her foolish choice to conceal the loss completely breaks her, making the ending tragic and ironic when Madame Forestier reveals, "Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!"

Ultimately, both stories offer timeless lessons that apply directly to life today. In modern society, people are constantly tempted by get-rich-quick schemes or driven to fake their wealth on social media just to impress others. Just like the Whites hoping for easy money from a cursed paw or Mathilde pretending to belong to high society, people today often risk their long-term well-being for temporary status. The shared theme in these works teaches us that actions driven by greed or superficial pride usually backfire, and taking responsibility for our choices is far better than suffering the painful consequences of trying to cheat reality.

In literature, characters often make quick decisions that end up completely changing their lives forever. Both "The Monkey's Paw" by W.W. Jacobs and "The Necklace" by Guy de Maupassant deal with the idea that our choices lead to heavy consequences. However, the theme of both stories is simply that borrowing an expensive necklace will make you poor, and finding an animal paw brings bad luck to your family. In "The Monkey's Paw," the Whites choose to mess with magical powers even after they are told not to. Jacobs connects his theme to older traditions like the Indian fakir and classic tales. The sergeant-major explains, "It had a spell put on it by an old fakir, a very holy man. This quote shows that an old fakir put a spell on it, which proves that interfering causes sorrow. Even when the soldier throws the paw into the fireplace, Mr. White still grabs it back. The soldier told him, "Better let it burn," which shows that fire is hot and burns dried objects. When they ignore him, Mrs. White mentions the Arabian Nights, which was an ancient comic book series about magical wishes that always had happy endings with no problems. Jacobs includes these references to show how foolish the Whites are for treating a dangerous warning like an entertaining fantasy.

Similarly, "The Necklace" shows how Madame Loisel makes foolish choices that completely ruin her future. Instead of admitting the truth when she loses her friend's jewelry, Mathilde and her husband decide to buy a secret replacement and take out huge loans. Guy de Maupassant writes, "She washed the dishes, using her dainty fingers and rosy nails on greasy pots and pans." This quote shows that Mathilde lost the necklace, proving her husband was working very hard at night doing accounts. Her choice to lie caused ten years of agony for no reason since the jewelry was actually fake.

In conclusion, both stories teach the reader that every action carries a serious consequence. People cannot just dodge fate or cover up their mistakes without paying a heavy price. However, the final central idea of both texts is that Mathilde lost a necklace and Mr. White lost his son. In the world today, this lesson is still very important because people make impulsive choices on social media or spend money they do not have on credit cards to impress others. If we try to take shortcuts instead of accepting our lives honestly, we can end up trapped in situations we cannot escape.

There are a lot of interesting stories that we read in English class about people who have things happen to them. In both "The Monkey's Paw" by W.W. Jacobs and "The Necklace" by Guy de Maupassant, the authors explore a powerful theme about choices and their consequences. Both stories demonstrate that when people make greedy or dishonest choices to change their status, they end up facing severe, unintended results that ruin their lives. Through the downfall of their characters, both authors show that interfering with reality and chasing after selfish desires always comes with a heavy price.

In "The Monkey's Paw," Jacobs shapes this theme by using elements from older storytelling traditions like the fakir's magic and the Arabian Nights. He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow." Mrs. White even jokes that the idea "Sounds like the Arabian Nights," referencing classic folklore where magical wishes usually backfire on foolish mortals. Instead of listening to Morris's warning to burn the paw, Mr. White makes the conscious choice to rescue it and wish for money. By drawing on ancient legends of fate and magic, Jacobs shows that human arrogance makes people believe they can escape the rules of the universe, but Mr. White's decision directly leads to the tragic loss of his only son.

Similarly, in "The Necklace," Madame Loisel's vain decisions bring about ten years of misery and suffering. Instead of being content with her comfortable middle-class life, she chooses to borrow a necklace to look wealthy at a party, and when she loses it, she chooses pride over honesty by hiding the truth. This choice forces her and her husband into massive debt, and Maupassant writes that "Thereafter Madame Loisel knew the horrible existence of the needy." Other times, people make reckless gambles hoping for easy rewards, ignoring clear warnings the way Mr. White ignored the sergeant-major.
